title: Stage 8, Lesson 9: Managing wealth across the stages of life
subtitle: The financial strategy that fits at 25 no longer fits at 55 - and that is entirely normal.
whyItMatters: Understanding how to adjust the strategy at each stage of life keeps you from applying one formula mechanically for a lifetime, and tells you when the approach needs to change.
openingQuestion: Why is a 25-year-old usually advised to accept a riskier portfolio (more equities) than a 58-year-old approaching retirement?
openingOptions: Because younger people generally hold considerably more spare cash than those about to reach the official retirement age
Because younger people are always more intelligent and better informed about investing than older people in today's society
Because there is no real difference to adjust for by age when building a personal investment portfolio
Because the young have time to recover and someone near retirement does not
explanation: The remaining time horizon is the core factor setting the appropriate level of risk. A young person has decades for a portfolio to recover from volatility; someone close to retirement has far less time, which is why the portfolio usually shifts gradually towards caution (more bonds) as the point of drawing on it approaches.

diagram.label: Early career: build the emergency fund, clear high-rate debt
Accumulation: a high equity weighting, contributing steadily
Approaching retirement: shift gradually into less volatile assets
After retirement: draw to a plan, keep an inflation defence

realWorldExample.company: Target-date funds (named for the expected retirement year)
realWorldExample.description: Many international retirement funds build portfolios that adjust automatically with the investor's age - the equity weighting falls and the bond weighting rises as the expected retirement year approaches, which is exactly the principle of reducing risk as the remaining time shortens.

quiz.question: Which stage of life is usually advised to prioritise an emergency fund and clearing high-rate debt over investing heavily in equities?
options: Already retired and living off the portfolio
Mid-career, with income now stable
Approaching retirement, when preserving capital matters most
Newly working, with no emergency fund yet
quiz.explanation: This follows the order of priorities from Stage 1: an emergency fund and high-rate debt come before heavy investing, at any age. Someone newly in work usually has neither foundation in place, so this is the stage for building basic financial safety before taking on higher risk.

quiz.question: Why should asset allocation be treated as a PROCESS that shifts over time rather than a decision made once?
options: Because circumstances change, so the appropriate level of risk changes too
Because markets change, so everything has to be bought and sold every month
Because the law on personal investing is amended fairly frequently
Because investment funds change their own portfolios continually
quiz.explanation: This is the difference between "rebalancing" (holding the target weights you chose, from Stage 7) and "adjusting strategy by life stage" (changing the target weights themselves as circumstances change) - both are necessary, but they serve different purposes.

quiz.question: What is the core factor setting the appropriate level of risk at each stage of life?
options: The absolute amount that person has accumulated so far
The time remaining before that money is needed
The monthly salary that person earns from their main job
The number of dependants that person supports in the household
quiz.explanation: Time is what decides whether you can recover from a fall. A 25-year-old and a 60-year-old with the same wealth and the same income should still hold very different portfolios for that reason.

quiz.question: What should the accumulation stage (roughly 25-45) prioritise most?
options: Maximising passive income immediately through dividends and rent
Preserving capital absolutely by putting the whole of your savings in the bank
Raising the savings rate and accepting volatility for long-run growth
Clearing every debt before starting any investment at all
quiz.explanation: This is the stage where time is most on your side, so volatility is not the enemy. What decides the outcome more than the choice of assets is the savings rate you can sustain.

quiz.question: What deserves particular attention in the pre-retirement stage (the last 5-10 working years)?
options: Stopping contributions, since the time left is too short to make a difference
Raising the equity weighting sharply to make up whatever the plan still lacks
Moving the entire portfolio into cash as soon as retirement is five years away
Reducing risk gradually, because a deep fall now has little time to recover
quiz.explanation: This is where sequence-of-returns risk is largest: the portfolio is at its biggest while the time to recover is at its shortest. Reducing risk gradually rather than cutting abruptly is the usual recommendation.

quiz.question: What is the common mistake during retirement itself?
options: Moving everything into assets that do not grow, letting inflation erode them
Keeping some equities in the portfolio rather than moving entirely into bonds
Drawing at a fixed rate and adjusting it for inflation each year
Keeping an emergency fund in cash equal to about a year of spending
quiz.explanation: Retiring at 60 means the portfolio still has 25-30 years of work to do. Trading volatility risk for the risk of running out is a bad exchange, because only the second one cannot be repaired.

keyTakeaways: The appropriate level of risk changes with the remaining time horizon - falling as the point of drawing on the money (retirement) approaches
The early career stage should prioritise the safety foundations (emergency fund, high-rate debt) before investing heavily
Asset allocation is a process of continual adjustment to circumstances, not a single decision

practicePrompt.question: Dat, 40, built an 80% equity portfolio at 25 and has never adjusted it in 15 years, even though retirement is now 15 years away rather than 35. Is that a sensible approach?
options: No - allocation needs continual adjustment; 80% equities fits at 25 but not with 15 years left
Yes, because once a good allocation has been chosen at 25 it should be held for life to maximise returns
Yes, because the time remaining until retirement has no bearing on the appropriate risk level of a portfolio
It does not matter, because asset allocation is a formality that does not affect the actual outcome
practicePrompt.explanation: The appropriate level of risk changes with the remaining time horizon - falling as the point of drawing on the money approaches - so the portfolio needs adjusting as circumstances change rather than being held fixed for life.

summary.keyIdea: The appropriate level of risk changes with the remaining time horizon - falling as the point of drawing on the money (retirement) approaches
summary.commonMistake: Reading the idea as a phrase to remember rather than as a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: The early career stage should prioritise the safety foundations (emergency fund, high-rate debt) before investing heavily

application.title: Assess yourself
application.message: Work out which stage you are in (newly working, mid-career, approaching retirement), then ask whether your current equity and bond weighting still fits the time horizon you have left.
application.secondary: The strategy that was right at 25 is not necessarily still right at 55.

sections.text: The financial strategy that fits at 25 no longer fits at 55 - and that is entirely normal. What sets the appropriate level of risk is not whether you enjoy taking chances, but the time horizon left before you need the money.
Early career: foundations first, higher risk afterwards

Someone newly in work, without an emergency fund and possibly still carrying high-rate consumer debt, should build the emergency fund and clear that debt before investing heavily in equities - exactly the order of priorities from Stage 1. This is not because youth matters less; it is because the safety foundation belongs before the higher risk.
The young have time to recover; those near retirement do not

A young investor has decades for a portfolio to recover from market falls, and can therefore carry a higher equity weighting. Someone close to retirement has far less time to wait out a large fall arriving just before they need to draw on the money, so the portfolio usually shifts gradually towards caution - more bonds - as that point approaches. Many international retirement funds (target-date funds) automate exactly this: the equity weighting falls and the bond weighting rises as the expected retirement year draws near.
Allocation is a process, not a one-off decision

This is the important distinction between "rebalancing" (holding the target weights you chose, from Stage 7) and "adjusting strategy by life stage" (changing the target weights themselves as circumstances change). Circumstances - age, the time left before the money is needed, family responsibilities - move over time, so the appropriate level of risk has to move with them. Both jobs are necessary, and they serve different purposes.

items: Early career: prioritise the emergency fund and high-rate debt, and start retirement investing early even with small amounts
Mid-career: raise the invested share, using the long horizon left to carry sensible risk
Approaching retirement: begin shifting towards a more cautious portfolio, reducing short-term volatility
Retired: keep some growth component to defend against inflation rather than moving 100% into cash and bonds
Review the whole allocation strategy whenever a major life change happens

lines: There is no portfolio that is "perfect forever" - only one that fits the person you are, at the stage of life you are living.
